findings.evidence: "[HYPOTHESIS] : guardrail latency (PII redaction, refusal checking) on generated 300‑token outputs, ~2–8 ms/request on CPU in the illustrative scenario; measure on the target stack"
findings.issue: Label-pair defect: this is a quantitative claim ("~2–8 ms/request") carrying only an Axis-2 tag ([HYPOTHESIS]) with no Axis-1 provenance tag, and it also calls itself "illustrative" without an [ILLUSTRATIVE] provenance tag. The Preface states a label pair always takes one item from each of the first two axes.
findings.fix_instruction: Tag the claim with a full pair, e.g. [ILLUSTRATIVE][HYPOTHESIS] (non-canonical worked figure, reasoned but unvalidated), and drop the redundant word "illustrative" from the sentence.

findings.evidence: "a low-batch (single-stream) decode rate of ~50 tokens/s on 8×H100 with a 70B FP16 model and 9.2K context for 300‑token outputs. The prefill phase (9.2K tokens) dominates TTFT: at ~1.08 s it leaves ~0.12 s against the 1.2 s budget — exactly the ~120 ms retrieval allocation, i.e. zero true headroom."
findings.issue: Prose ambiguity: "The prefill phase ... dominates TTFT" is immediately qualified by "at ~1.08 s it leaves ~0.12 s", but the sentence does not name the retrieval term as the subtracted quantity until the clause after the dash. A reader can momentarily read "1.08 s dominates TTFT" as a claim that prefill is the whole TTFT, contradicting the TTFTe2e formula (retrieval + admission/queue + tokenization/transfer + prefill) defined in Ch 2 and Ch 4.
findings.fix_instruction: Rewrite as: "Within the 1.2 s TTFT budget, prefill is allocated ~1.08 s and retrieval ~120 ms, leaving zero true headroom on the two-term model (admission/queue and tokenization/transfer are outside it)."

findings.evidence: Page 115 Table 5-1 note: "FLOPs per embedding = 2 × params × L at a 64-token query (L = 64) ... Note: 2 × params × L treats the token-embedding table as a per-position matmul; it is a lookup, so the proxy overstates compute — most for the smallest model (MiniLM's table is ~51% of its params). Body-parameter ratios are the truer cross-model comparison (mpnet/MiniLM ≈7.7× body-only vs 4.8× by total params ...)."
findings.issue: Recompute the FLOPs column: MiniLM ~23M → 2 × 23e6 × 64 = 2.944 GFLOPs ≈ 2.9 ✓; mpnet ~110M → 2 × 110e6 × 64 = 14.08 ≈ 14 ✓; bge-large ~335M → 2 × 335e6 × 64 = 42.88 ≈ 43 ✓. Ratios: mpnet/MiniLM total = 110/23 = 4.78 ≈ 4.8× ✓; body-only 86.6/11.3 = 7.66 ≈ 7.7× ✓; bge-large/mpnet = 335/110 = 3.05 ≈ 3× ✓. The defect is a labelling/register problem: the table's column is headed 'GFLOPs per embedding (64-token query)' but the note admits the figure is 'a proxy [that] overstates compute' and that 'the proxy ratio (4.8×) is a lower bound on the true body-only compute ratio (≈7.7×), not an upper bound' — a quantity whose direction of bias is opposite to its own label ('per embedding' reads as a measurement-grade cost). The column heading does not say 'proxy' and the table's three rows carry no per-row provenance tag; the whole table is untagged in the caption.
findings.fix_instruction: Rename the column to 'GFLOPs per embedding (64-token query) — proxy' and add a table-level provenance line ('[1P][FACT] parameter counts and dimensions from model cards; [1P][DERIVED] FLOP proxy') so the register of the column is unambiguous.

findings.evidence: Page 116: "[HYPOTHESIS] : within a given embedding family or a controlled dimensionality experiment, reducing the embedding dimension may trade retrieval quality for lower index storage and query-time projection cost ... e.g. a 384-dim variant of the same model family can halve the index storage of a 768-dim one (the encoder's compute is essentially unchanged, since only the final projection shrinks)." And: "Assume, as a scenario input rather than a measured result, a quality-vs-dimension uplift of up to ~15% MAP (an assumption, not a cited finding — no study is invoked here)".
findings.issue: The ~15% MAP figure is explicitly labelled 'a scenario input' and 'an assumption, not a cited finding', but it is written inline in the same bracket as a [HYPOTHESIS] tag and is then used as the decisive input for the chapter's recommendation (p. 116: 'the top-of-range ~15% MAP gain (a [HYPOTHESIS] scenario input ... ) translates into sufficient answer-quality improvement to justify the ~7.7× body-only FLOP cost'). Under the book's own Axis-2 definitions (p. 17), a 'deliberately chosen scenario input' is [ASSUMPTION], paired with a scenario provenance ([canonical scenario] or [ILLUSTRATIVE]) — not [HYPOTHESIS], and the Preface is explicit (p. 17): 'a hypothesis is tagged [HYPOTHESIS] (Axis 2), never [ILLUSTRATIVE] (Axis 1)'. Here a scenario input is tagged [HYPOTHESIS] with no provenance tag, which is a label/axis mismatch under the book's own rules.
findings.fix_instruction: Tag the ~15% MAP input as [ILLUSTRATIVE][ASSUMPTION] (a chosen scenario input) and reserve [HYPOTHESIS] for the untested claim that it transfers to the target corpus; keep the two adjacent but distinct labels so the recommendation's dependence on an assumed number is visible.

findings.evidence: Page 117, Table 5-2 rows: "Output tokens per dollar (single-stream decode, 50 tok/s) | 9,000 output tokens per dollar | 50 tok/s × 3600 s/hr ÷ $20/hr [ILLUSTRATIVE][DERIVED]"; "Total tokens per dollar (single-stream decode + overlapped prefill; not the 10 rps fleet point) | ~285,000 tokens per dollar at 300 output tokens/request | 50 × (1 + 9,200/300) ≈ 1,583 tok/s × 3600 ÷ $20 [ILLUSTRATIVE][DERIVED]"; "Total tokens per dollar (serial single-stream floor, no overlap; 20 ms/token basis) | ~242,000 tokens per dollar (~199,000 at the canonical 25 ms/token) | 9,500/7.08 ≈ 1,342 tok/s × 3600 ÷ $20; 7.08 s = 1.08 s prefill + 6.0 s decode at the illustrative 20 ms/token rate; at the canonical 25 ms/token, 9,500/8.58 ≈ 1,107 tok/s ≈ 199,000 tokens/$ [ILLUSTRATIVE][DERIVED]"
findings.issue: Recompute: 50 × 3600/20 = 9,000 ✓. 50 × (1 + 30.667) = 1,583.3 → ×3600/20 = 285,000 ✓. 9,500/7.08 = 1,341.8 → ×180 = 241,530 ≈ 242,000 ✓. 9,500/8.58 = 1,107.2 → ×180 = 199,300 ≈ 199,000 ✓. The arithmetic is sound. The defect is that the third row's cell carries two different operating points (20 ms/token and 25 ms/token) and two different derived numbers inside a single cell, and the second row is labelled 'not the 10 rps fleet point' — but the table's verdict row below says 'Embedding: all-mpnet-base-v2 (768-dim); Generation: 70B FP16 on 8×H100' with no pointer that these per-dollar figures apply to a single stream, not to the fleet the rest of the book sizes. The chapter does add a reconciliation note (p. 119) that warns 'Do not pair a batched whole-fleet numerator with a per-host single-stream denominator' — but the table itself, whose rows are the numbers a reader will quote, carries the single-stream basis only in one row's parenthetical.
findings.fix_instruction: Add a table-level basis note in Table 5-2 stating that all four per-dollar rows are single-stream (batch-1-equivalent) per-host figures on an illustrative 50 tok/s rate, and are floors rather than the host's batched serving rate — so no row can be lifted as the fleet's economics.

findings.evidence: Page 120: "Because this workload is input-heavy (9.2K input vs 300 output tokens), the prefill leg consumes ~97% of the tokens per request (9,200 ÷ 9,500) — and, because each prefill token runs the full 2 × 70B forward FLOP, it is also ~97% of the linear forward-FLOP cost (before the quadratic attention term). But it is only ~15% of the wall-clock time (1.08 s prefill vs 6.0 s decode) ... decode dominates single-stream wall-clock (~85% of 1.08 s + 6.0 s at this 20 ms/token rate; ~87% of 8.58 s at the canonical 25 ms/token rate, Ch 4)".
findings.issue: Recompute: 9,200/9,500 = 96.8% ≈ 97% ✓. 1.08/(1.08+6.0) = 15.25% ≈ 15% ✓. 6.0/7.08 = 84.7% ≈ 85% ✓. 7.5/8.58 = 87.4% ≈ 87% ✓. All correct. The defect is that the ~85% figure uses the illustrative 20 ms/token decode rate while the ~97% FLOP figure and the canonical scenario use the 25 ms/token basis; the sentence mixes bases in a single parenthetical without flagging that the 85% and 87% are different operating points of the same quantity. This is the same basis-mixing the book warns against elsewhere (p. 119: 'The three figures are stated on different bases and are not one series'), applied here inside one sentence.
findings.fix_instruction: Split the parenthetical so the illustrative 20 ms/token figure and the canonical 25 ms/token figure are each labeled with their basis (as the p. 119 reconciliation note does for the three per-dollar figures), rather than appearing as two unlabelled percentages of the same quantity.

findings.evidence: Page 122: "Q∗ = (Ctrain + Cweights-extra) / (∆Q · value per corrected query)" and the note: "Note: this formula captures only the one-time training and carry cost amortized against the quality uplift; it omits the recurring per-query prefill/retrieval saving that fine-tuning's shorter context (§5.3(c)) would confer, so it yields an upper bound on the true break-even volume — a conservative (higher) estimate of the queries needed to justify fine-tuning, in favour of RAG + guardrails, because omitting fine-tuning's recurring saving understates its benefit."
findings.issue: The formula is dimensionally fine but the note's conclusion is logically wrong as written: if fine-tuning's recurring saving is omitted, the numerator is understated, so Q∗ is UNDERstated (a lower break-even) — i.e. the computed value is a LOWER bound on the true break-even, not an upper bound, and it favours fine-tuning, not RAG + guardrails. The text says the opposite ('yields an upper bound ... in favour of RAG + guardrails'). This is a direct arithmetic-logic inversion: a smaller numerator gives a smaller quotient.
findings.fix_instruction: Correct the note: omitting fine-tuning's recurring per-query saving understates its benefit and therefore UNDERstates the break-even volume (a lower bound), which biases the comparison toward fine-tuning. Rewrite the sentence to say 'yields a lower bound on the true break-even volume, i.e. it is conservative in favour of fine-tuning; including fine-tuning's recurring saving raises Q∗'.

findings.evidence: Page 128, Fig 5.1 caption: "figure 5.1: Model selection for RAG: workload → five selection surfaces → two legs (retrieval/embedding, generation/70B) → the system decision. The first four surfaces are model-selection dimensions; the fifth, retrieve-vs-generate, is a system split rather than a model choice. All five are deliberately distinct from the end-to-end evaluation gates (retrieval quality, reranking, embedding recall, grounding, and final answer quality) that a RAG system must also pass — those gates are measured on the target corpus and are not shown here because this figure is a selection map, not an evaluation pipeline. [ILLUSTRATIVE conceptual]"
findings.issue: The figure is a selection map whose output box reads 'RAG system decision → base + RAG + guardrails' — but the figure's own caption says the evaluation gates (including 'final answer quality') are 'not shown here because this figure is a selection map, not an evaluation pipeline'. The chapter's own takeaway (p. 122) says the RAG+guardrails default is 'conditional on lying below Q∗' and that the quality gap is 'unverified'. A figure that outputs a decision ('base + RAG + guardrails') while its caption disclaims the gate that would validate it presents a conclusion as more settled than the chapter allows — the figure has no 'provisional' or 'pending validation' marker on its output box.
findings.fix_instruction: Mark the figure's decision box as provisional (e.g. 'base + RAG + guardrails — provisional; Q∗ unmeasured (§5.3(c))') so the figure matches the chapter's stated conditionality, and add the evaluation-gate boxes as a dashed 'not evaluated here' input if the diagram permits.

findings.evidence: Page 116: "[ILLUSTRATIVE][DERIVED]: for a 1 M-chunk corpus (a Ch 5-local illustrative input, not part of Table 4-2), the index storage for a D-dim float32 vector corpus is bytes = nchunks × D × 4 ... For 768-dim: 1×106 × 768 × 4 = 3.07 GB; for 384-dim: 1×106 × 384 × 4 = 1.54 GB; a difference of ~1.5 GB. At 10× the corpus (10 M chunks), that difference grows to ~15 GB."
findings.issue: Recompute: 1e6 × 768 × 4 = 3.072e9 B = 3.07 GB ✓; 1e6 × 384 × 4 = 1.536e9 = 1.54 GB ✓; difference 1.536 GB ≈ 1.5 GB ✓; at 10× = 15.36 GB ≈ 15 GB ✓. The arithmetic is correct. The defect is register honesty in the opposite direction from the usual: this input (1 M chunks) is a scenario input, so the derived storage should be [ILLUSTRATIVE][DERIVED] — correct as tagged. But the Ch. 5 mini-case (p. 126) then states '~3.1 GB index storage for a 1 M-chunk corpus (vs ~1.5 GB at 384-dim)' with NO tag, presenting a chapter-local illustrative input as an unmarked fact in the scenario narrative, and also as a number that 'scales with corpus size, alongside the 70B base model' — a comparison the mini-case then does not make quantitative (the 70B weights are 140 GB, the index 3.1 GB).
findings.fix_instruction: Carry the [ILLUSTRATIVE] provenance into the mini-case's index-storage sentence and state explicitly that the 1 M-chunk corpus size is a chapter-local input, not part of Table 4-2's canonical set, as §5.3.1 already does.

findings.evidence: Page 122: "Fine-tuning does not make the model smaller — pruning is a separate operation. A full fine-tune keeps the ~140 GB 70B weight set (and adds a checkpoint), while a LoRA adapter is tiny but does not change the live weight footprint. Consequently the latency effect of fine-tuning is not 'smaller effective model' and cannot be assumed to cut TTFT; any TTFT change must be measured."
findings.issue: The paragraph is careful and correct. The defect is upstream: the same chapter's §5.3.3 heading presents 'Paradigm 2 — Fine-tuned model on domain-specific Q-A pairs' as the alternative to RAG, and the section never says what a fine-tuned model actually *is* in deployment terms for this workload (a merged checkpoint vs a served adapter), which it partly defers to a parenthetical in §5.5 (p. 124: 'whereas a merged/fully-fine-tuned model of identical architecture need not change the inference shape'). The section therefore introduces the fine-tuning option without stating the operational difference (a checkpoint to build, promote and roll back, per Ch. 21's model lifecycle) that the Architecture Consequence and the ADR will need — a gap rather than an arithmetic error.
findings.fix_instruction: Add one sentence in §5.3.3 naming the deployment artifact each paradigm produces (a merged checkpoint for full fine-tuning; an adapter or merged checkpoint for LoRA) and pointing to Ch. 21's lifecycle and Ch. 18's model-registry implications, so the selection chapter's two paradigms are operationalized before the fleet chapters.

findings.evidence: Page 119: "Every per-dollar figure in this chapter inherits that assumption, so each is an analytical bound, not a benchmark." Page 120: "[ILLUSTRATIVE][DERIVED]: tokens/s per dollar with prefill included. (Mixed-input convention: when a derivation mixes a canonical price with an illustrative rate, the result carries the non-canonical provenance — here the 50 tok/s rate input is [ILLUSTRATIVE][ASSUMPTION] while the $20/hr price is canonical (Table 4‑2, a dated price snapshot, [canonical scenario][ASSUMPTION]).)"
findings.issue: The 'mixed-input convention' is stated as a rule in Ch. 5 but appears nowhere in the Preface's evidence-discipline section, which defines the two axes and the label-pair rule without any convention for derivations that mix provenances. A reader working from the Preface alone would not know how to label such a result, and the convention is applied to different quantities on p. 117 ('the non-canonical input wins') and p. 120 ('the result carries the non-canonical provenance') — consistent in effect, but the rule itself is undocumented in the normative section.
findings.fix_instruction: Add the mixed-input convention to the Preface's evidence-discipline panel (Axis 1 note) as a named rule, so a deriver's labelling choice is governed by the front matter rather than introduced mid-chapter.

findings.evidence: Page 119: "the ~50 tok/s used here is a deliberately low-batch (single-stream) generation rate — conservative against batched serving rates, and faster than the canonical 40 tok/s batch-1 budget point (25 ms/token) without contradicting it."
findings.issue: The statement 'faster than the canonical 40 tok/s batch-1 budget point (25 ms/token) without contradicting it' is asserted but not demonstrated: 50 tok/s = 20 ms/token, and the chapter's own next sentence explains why 20 ms/token is achievable without batching — 'the same host's per-GPU shard batch-1 weight-read floor is only ~5.2 ms/token (17.5 GB per GPU shard ÷ 3.35 TB/s, Ch 2)'. But the canonical 25 ms TPOT budget includes attention over a 9.2K-token KV cache, the TP all-reduce, sampling and scheduling, all of which the book says must be measured (p. 50, p. 137). So the claim that 50 tok/s 'without contradicting' the 25 ms budget is true only for the weight-read term alone, and the paragraph's own reasoning shows a 5.2 ms floor that would admit ~190 tok/s on the weight term — meaning the 50 tok/s point is an arbitrarily chosen illustrative value, not a measured or derived one.
findings.fix_instruction: State explicitly that 50 tok/s is a chosen illustrative point (not derived from the 5.2 ms weight-read floor, and not a measurement), so the reader does not treat the paragraph as having justified it from the hardware arithmetic.

findings.evidence: p.125: '[HYPOTHESIS] : the interaction between embedding dimension and retrieval quality across diverse enterprise domains is not yet characterized with reproducible benchmarks.' (three §5.7 bullets carry bare [HYPOTHESIS] with no Axis-1 tag); p.146: 'it changes what must be inventoried before that budget's arithmetic is reused for a different generation mechanism. [DERIVED]' and 'Static prompt embeddings can remain reusable, but that is not the growing autoregressive cache. [DERIVED]'; p.175: 'Profile the actual position count before quoting FLOPs. [DERIVED]'; pp.113–114: methodological statements closed with '[1P][DERIVED]' (e.g. 'Chapter 14 §14.4 ... supplies the acceptance test. [1P][DERIVED]'); Preface p.17: 'Every load-bearing quantitative claim carries Axes 1 and 2 as an inline pair (e.g. [1P][DERIVED])'
findings.issue: Evidence-tag drift against the book's own rules: (a) §5.7's [HYPOTHESIS] claims carry only the epistemic axis, with no paired provenance tag; (b) the Ch. 7/Ch. 8 caveat boxes close qualitative mechanism statements with a bare [DERIVED] even though nothing was 'computed by arithmetic from stated inputs' (DERIVED's definition); (c) §5.1.1–5.1.2 tag non-arithmetic methodology statements [1P][DERIVED]. The Preface requires a full Axis-1+Axis-2 pair for claims and reserves DERIVED for arithmetic.
findings.fix_instruction: Pair each claim tag with an Axis-1 provenance (e.g. [canonical scenario][DERIVED] where the statement derives from canonical inputs), delete [DERIVED] from non-quantitative sentences, and re-tag the §5.1/§5.7 methodological and hypothesis statements with the correct axis pair (or no tag). Recurrence-sweep §7.3.2, §8.1.1–8.3.1 for the same bare-tag pattern.
